newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says NATO should name second wave members.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says NATO should name second wave members.

text.p: Hungary's foreign minister said on Tuesday he would prefer NATO to name not just a first group of new members at its Madrid summit next week but also all the countries that would make up the second wave of enlargement.

"I would find it good if the Madrid summit would name those that could join (NATO) in the second wave, maybe even giving a time frame," Laszlo Kovacs told Hungarian diplomats at a Budapest conference.

Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic were named by the United States earlier this month as the countries Washington would like to see invited in Madrid as the first group of new NATO members drawn from the dozen states which have applied.
But France and several other southern European members have fought strongly for the inclusion of Romania and Slovenia and have been angered by the U.S. preference for only the leading three.
Kovacs said that it would be premature to rule out the acceptance of Slovenia and Romania. "While the U.S.'s word is decisive, it is not exclusive," Kovacs said.
He also said that when the decision on the new entrants is taken, NATO should make it clear why other applicants were refused.
"NATO should send a clear message as to why they did not make it and what these countries have to do in order to join NATO, and also help them achieve the conditions of NATO accession," Kovacs said.
He added that once the Madrid summit announced the countries that would join NATO in the first round, Hungary would have to pay special attention to its relations with those left out.
But the failure of other applicants to get into NATO now would not have a negative effect on Hungary's relations with them.
"They all know that Hungary did everything in its power to promote their accession," Kovacs said.
He said that if Hungary is named in the first group he expected accession talks to be finished by December or even earlier.
"Some NATO sources I have talked to suggest the accession talks could take as little as two months."
He added that he did not go along with western fears over the cost of NATO expansion and added that enlargement is the cheapest way to guarantee the region's security.
"The international community already spent more money in Bosnia than the cost of a (limited) NATO expansion would be."
